newsitem.title: USA: Cow carcasses a problem? compost.
newsitem.headline: Cow carcasses a problem? compost.

text.p: With hundreds of thousands of dead cattle piling up in the Dakotas due to recent blizzards, cattle ranchers are being encouraged to try a new way to get rid of the carcasses: composting.

John Hoehne and Charles Fulhage, agricultural engineers at the University of Missouri, said on Friday that South Dakota officials have shown interest in their method of using sawdust compost heaps to break down large farm animal carcasses.
A beef carcass "may take a year ... but it'll work," Hoehne said.
The process consists of covering dead animals with about 12 inches (30 cm) of sawdust and then waiting as temperatures in the compost heap reach 140 to 160 degrees Farenheit (60-71 degrees Celsius).
"You can put a 400-pound (181 kg) sow in there," Hoehne said, "and after six months you won't find anything except maybe one or two of the big bones, and they'll be soft."

Under South Dakota law, producers may only dispose of dead animals by burying, burning or by sending them to rendering facilities. But Fulhage and Hoehne said the state may allow the composting alternative after thousands of cattle died as a result of recent blizzards.
Charles Seagren, assistant state veterinarian in South Dakota, said the large number of carcasses could pose environmental and aesthetic problems when the spring thaw arrives.
Hoehne and Fulhage said the technique began on the East Coast, where large-scale poultry producers had to dispose of hundreds of pounds of small bird carcasses each day.
